title: Soil_Moisture_Alaska_ Alberta_2123
abstract: This dataset comprises 1 hour in-situ soil moisture recordings obtained from data loggers stationed primarily in organic soils (characterized by very low bulk density) at two specific locations: 1) along the Sag River in Alaska, U.S., and 2) near Red Earth Creek in Alberta, Canada. Alongside soil moisture probe intervals, the dataset contains temperature probe data, along with calibration coefficients and soil pro measurements utilized in establishing per-probe calibrations for deriving volumetric moisture content. The data loggers employed were Campbell Scientific CR200 models equipped with CS625 water content reflectometers and temperature probe 109. More detailed information on the calibration derivation process is available in a supplementary document. The primary objective of this dataset is to furnish field measurements suitable for calibrating and validating satellite-based soil moisture retrieval algorithms. Spanning from July 2017 to July 2021, the dataset encompasses occasional interruptions and is presented in comma-separated values (CSV) format.

abstract: This data set includes measurements of soil carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrous oxide (N2O) concentrations, as well as soil volumetric water content (VWC) from a rainfall exclusion experiment conducted at the km 67 Seca Floresta site in the Tapajos National Forest, Brazil. title: LBACD04METFLUXES _946
abstract: Tower flux measurements of carbon dioxide, water vapor, heat, and meteorological variables were obtained at the Tapajos National Forest, km 83 site, Santarem, Para, Brazil. For the period from June 29, 2000, to March 11, 2004, data includes 30-minute averages and calculated quantities of fluxes of momentum, heat, water vapor, and carbon dioxide, as well as the storage of carbon dioxide in the air column. The data is provided in three comma-separated s: 30-minute averages, 1 day (24-hour) averages, 1 month (calendar) averages. The measurements taken from the 67 m tower cover variables related to meteorology, soil moisture, respiration, fluxes of momentum, heat, water vapor, and carbon dioxide. These measurements were used to calculate the storage of carbon dioxide, Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE), and Gross Primary Productivity (GPP).

title: CD04_SOILMOISTURE _979
abstract: This data set includes continuous high-resolution frequency-domain reflectometry measurements of soil moisture to a depth of 10 meters and precipitation data from two towers at the km 83 tower site (logged forest site) in the Tapajos National Forest, Para, Brazil. Measurements were taken during 2002 and 2003. The data is provided in two comma-delimited ASCII s. The first tower, referred to as the 'intact' tower, was installed in an undisturbed forest area in June 2000. It was equipped for eddy flux and micrometeorological measurements and operated for 15 months before any logging occurred in the area. The second tower, known as the 'gap tower', was installed and began operating in June 2002, 400 meters east of the intact tower, in the center of a 50 m x 50 m log landing. Soil moisture measurements were taken in 10-meter-deep vertical pits (1 x 1 m²) approximately 20 meters from the micrometeorological tower sites in undisturbed forest patches. Reflectometers were inserted horizontally into shaft walls at depth of 0.15, 0.30, 0.60, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 10 meters below the surface.

title: ND07_NO_FLUX_ CERRADO_1124
abstract: This dataset presents measurements of soil nitric oxide (NO) flux, soil moisture, and soil nitrate (NO3) and ammonium (NH4) concentrations in Cerrado soils subjected to nitrogen fertilization. Data were collected from both control and fertilized experimental plots within the Ecological Reserve of the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) in Brasilia, Brazil, from March 26, 2004, to November 25, 2004. The soils had been receiving nitrogen and phosphorus fertilization treatments since 1998. The project's goal was to assess the long-term effects of nutrient addition (N and N+P) on nitrogen oxide emissions from soil to the atmosphere in a native Cerrado area. This dataset includes one comma-delimited (csv) ASCII .

title: CD09_SOILS_VEG _TAPAJOS_1104
abstract: This data set comprises manual measurements of trace gas fluxes, including carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and nitric oxide, at undisturbed and logged forest sites in the Tapajos National Forest, near Santarem, Para, Brazil. At both undisturbed and logged sites, manual measurements were taken approximately weekly. At the undisturbed sites, fluxes from clay and sand soils were measured. At the logged sites, fluxes were measured at the deck (patio), skid trail, clearing, and forest areas. Additionally, 1 day average water-filled pore space (WFPS) data for clay and sand soils in the undisturbed forest are included.

abstract: This data set includes the results of soil sample analyses for nitrate (NO3) and physical properties, collected over one year following reduced impact logging at the Fazenda Rohsamar in the municipality of Juruena, northwestern Mato Grosso. Sample locations were randomly selected from stratified regions of the 1,400 ha Block 5 to account for local soil variability. Soil samples were collected to a depth of 8 meters in (1) nine gaps formed by single tree removal, and (2) nine areas of undisturbed primary forest. The undisturbed forest areas were within patches of Block 5 that were protected from logging. Additionally, three forested areas with high sand content were sampled to a depth of 3 meters.

title: TG08_SOIL_GAS_ WETTING_1101
abstract: This data set includes measurements of soil gas fluxes of nitric oxide (NO), nitrous oxide (N2O), and carbon dioxide (CO2), along with soil moisture, soil temperature, and soil pools of ammonium and nitrate in response to a simulated rain event. The study was conducted in August 1998 during the dry season at Fazenda Nova Vida, Rondonia in the Brazilian Amazon. The research sites included soils from mature forests and pastures of two different ages (11 and 26 years old). The data is provided in a single comma-delimited ASCII . This study aimed to understand how changes in soil moisture (specifically, rains at the end of the dry season) influenced the fluxes of NO, N2O, and CO2 from forest and pasture soils in the southwestern Brazilian Amazon (Garcia-Montiel et al., 2003). The main objectives were to measure the short-term dynamics of soil emissions of NO, N2O, and CO2 in forest and pasture soils following soil wetting after prolonged dryness, and to quantify the contribution of the resulting pulses of nitrogen oxide fluxes to dry season and annual fluxes.

title: MD_CD03_MESOSCALE _944
abstract: A mesoscale network has been established in the Santarem region of Para, Brazil, comprising eight meteorological stations: Belterra, Km 117 (Fazenda Sr. Davi), Mojui, Jamaraqua, Guarana, Embrapa (Cacoal Grande), Vila Franca, and Sudam (Curua Una). Data collection began almost continuously at Belterra and Km 117 in August 1998. Mojui, Jamaraqua, and Guarana stations started data collection in July 2000, while Embrapa, Vila Franca, and Sudam stations began in 2002. The dataset is organized into 52 individual comma-separated ASCII s, with each representing one calendar year of data from one site. The names clearly indicate the site and year, and all s follow a consistent header format and organizational structure. Measurements include air temperature, air pressure, wind speed and direction, relative humidity, downward solar radiation, and, at some stations, soil temperature and moisture.

title: CD08_Ecosystem_Resp _Manaus_912
abstract: Leaf, live wood (tree stem), and soil respiration were measured along with additional environmental factors over a one-year period in a Central Amazon terra firme forest. This data is provided in three comma-delimited s. The investigations took place at an INPA reserve along the ZF2 road at km 34 [LBA 34] on two permanent forest inventory plots, known as the Jacaranda plots (-2.6091 degrees S, -60.2093 degrees W), each measuring 20 x 2500 meters. These long and narrow plots capture ecosystem variation associated with the undulating local topography. Additionally, leaf respiration measurements were taken at a tower located at ZF-2 road (km 14 [LBA 14]). Leaf respiration was measured in July and August 2001, woody respiration in August 2000 and June 2001, and soil respiration between July 2000 and June 2001 at 4 to 6-week intervals. Understanding how the carbon balance of tropical forests will respond to global change requires knowledge of individual heterotrophic and autotrophic respiratory sources, as well as the factors that control respiratory variability.

title: CD03_PASTURE_FLUX _962
abstract: This dataset compiles carbon and energy eddy covariance flux, meteorology, radiation, canopy temperature, humidity, CO2 pros, and soil moisture and temperature pro data collected at nine towers across the Brazilian Amazon. The data, spanning from 1999 to 2006, were provided by various independent investigators from different flux tower projects. This is Version 2 of the dataset, which includes harmonized data across projects, additional quality control checks, and aggregation to 1 hour, 1 day, 16-day, and 1 month timesteps. It aims to facilitate integrative studies and data-model synthesis from a common reference point. The dataset comprises 36 tab-delimited (*.txt) data s and a companion , CD32_Fluxes_Brazil-Readme.pdf. Each of the nine towers has four s with data aggregated to 1 hour, 1 day, 16-day, and 1 month intervals.

abstract: This dataset features vegetation community characteristics and biophysical data collected in 2018 from regions impacted by wildfires in 2014 and 2015, along with data from nine unburned validation sites in the Northwest Territories, Canada. In addition, soil moisture measurements were collected to validate UAVSAR airborne data, and the depth to frozen ground was measured at the nine unburned sites. This 2018 fieldwork marks the culmination of four years of field sampling in the wildfire-affected areas

title: FLUXNET_Canada_1335
abstract: FLUXNET Canada was a research network operating from 1993 to 2014, consisting of the Fluxnet-Canada Research Network (FCRN) and the Canadian Carbon Program (CCP). This national network included university and government scientists studying the effects of climate and disturbances on carbon cycling across an east-west transect of Canadian forest and peatland ecosystems. The dataset includes measured and modeled results from site investigators, although the data were not standardized or quality-controlled. The dataset contains: Atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapor fluxes, Various ancillary meteorological variables, Soil CO2 efflux and soil moisture, Stable carbon isotopes, Soil and vegetation characteristics. Additionally, the dataset includes documentation and descriptions for the 32 tower sites across 12 flux research stations. The time span of the data is from 1993 to 2014, although most sites do not have continuous data coverage for the entire period.

title: Wildfires_2014_NWT_ Canada_1307
abstract: This dataset offers comprehensive information regarding peatland landcover classifications, fire progression, and vegetation community biophysical data derived from areas affected by a wildfire in 2014 within the Northwest Territories, Canada. The peatland maps provide classification of peatland types (such as bog, fen, marsh, swamp) along with the level of biomass (open or forested). Additionally, the fire progression maps enable the assessment of wildfire advancement rates on a 1 day time scale. Field data, gathered in 2015, encompasses evaluations of burn severity, woody seedling/sprouting observations, soil moisture measurements, and assessments of tree diameter and height within the burned sites. Similar vegetation characterization is conducted at landcover validation sites to enhance the dataset's reliability and accuracy.

title: Southern_Boreal_Plot_Attribute_1740
abstract: This dataset presents the results of field measurements and estimates of carbon stocks and combustion rates in burned and unburned southern boreal forest stands near La Ronge and Weyakwin in central Saskatchewan, Canada. The data were collected in 2016 at 47 stands affected by the 2015 Saskatchewan wildfires (Egg, Philion, and Brady) and 32 adjacent unburned stands. The characterization of these stands involved field observations and sampling of the vegetative community (including tree species, abundance, biophysical measurements, stand age, coarse woody debris, and fire or logging history), soil properties (such as soil moisture class, unburned and burned soil organic layer depth, and samples for bulk density and carbon analysis), and basic landscape geophysical traits.

title: BOREAS_TE20SLDN_356
abstract: This dataset encompasses the major soil properties of samples collected at the tower flux sites in the Northern Study Area (NSA). The soil samples were gathered by Hugo Veldhuis and his team from the University of Manitoba. The mineral soil samples were primarily analyzed by Barry Goetz under Dr. Harold Rostad's supervision at the University of Saskatchewan, while the organic soil samples were analyzed by Peter Haluschak under Hugo Veldhuis's supervision at the Centre for Land and Biological Resources Research in Winnipeg, Manitoba. During field investigations and mapping, selected surface and subsurface soil samples were collected for laboratory analysis, serving as benchmark references for specific soil attributes in general soil characterization. Detailed soil sampling, descriptions, and laboratory analyses were conducted on selected modal soils to provide examples of common soil physical and chemical characteristics in the study area.

title: ABoVE_Plot_Data_ Burned_Sites_1744
abstract: This dataset synthesizes field plot characterization data, derived above-ground and below-ground combusted carbon, and components of the Fire Weather Index (FWI) System for burned boreal forest sites across Alaska, USA, the Northwest Territories, and Saskatchewan, Canada, spanning from 1983 to 2016. Unburned plot data are also included. The compiled plot-level data encompass stand age, disturbance history, tree density, and tree biophysical measurements to calculate above-ground (AG) and below-ground (BG) biomass/carbon pools, pre-fire and residual post-fire soil organic layer (SOL) depth, and combustion estimates for tree structural classes. Additionally, the measured slope and aspect for each site and an assigned moisture class based on topography are provided. The dataset includes information from 1019 burned and 152 unburned sites. From the derived AG and BG carbon pools and SOL losses, total carbon combusted, the proportion of pre-fire carbon combusted, and the proportion of total carbon combusted were calculated for each plot. FWI System components, such as moisture and drought codes and indices of fire danger, were obtained for each plot from existing data sources based on the plot location, year of burn, and a dynamic start-up date (day of burn, DOB) from the global fire weather database. Data for soil characteristics are included in a separate.

title: CTP_SMTMN
abstract: The CTP-SMTMN network was established through three field campaigns during the summers of 2010 to 2012, resulting in a total of 57 stations at an average elevation of 4650 m MSL. These stations measure soil moisture and temperature and are organized into three nested networks: the large network, the medium network, and the small network. These networks support different scales of land hydrological modeling and microwave retrievals. All stations are located on grasslands, taking into account various microscale factors to ensure representativeness. Wetlands are excluded from the network due to high maintenance costs, but their regional soil moisture contribution is considered through spatial upscaling.

title: HiWATER_EHWSN
abstract: EcoHydrological Wireless Sensor Network (EHWSN) is installed in the middle reach of the Heihe River Basin. The EHWSN has two main objectives: first, to capture the multiscale spatial variations and temporal dynamics of soil moisture, soil temperature, and land surface temperature in heterogeneous farmland; and second, to provide a ground-truth estimate for remote sensing at an approximate kilometer pixel scale using spatial upscaling. This ground truth is essential for validating and evaluating remote-sensing products. The EHWSN uses distributed observation nodes to create an automated, intelligent, and remotely controllable network, enhancing integrated, standardized, and automated observations for hydrological and ecological research at the basin scale.

title: TAHMO
abstract: The idea behind this initiative is to develop a dense network of hydro-meteorological monitoring stations in sub-Saharan Africa, with one station every 30 km. This involves installing 20,000 stations across the continent. By utilizing innovative sensor technology and ICT, TAHMO stations are designed to be both inexpensive and robust. The stations are placed at schools and integrated into educational programs, enriching the curriculum and fostering a new generation of scientists. Local weather data is combined with models and satellite observations to gain insights into the distribution of water and energy stocks and fluxes.

title: HOBE
abstract: The Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity Mission (SMOS) collects global surface soil moisture data every three days. Validating these products across diverse climates and environments is essential. To support this, a soil moisture and temperature sensor network was established in the Skjern River Catchment, Denmark. This article aims to describe the network's implementation for SMOS validation and present sample data to verify the method. The network design involved selecting a representative SMOS pixel (44 × 44 km) with minimal water impact, arranging three network clusters along a precipitation gradient, and distributing stations based on prevailing environmental conditions. Data collected showed moisture and temperature patterns related to land cover and soil conditions, with 0?5 cm soil moisture measurements influenced by soil texture. Regional differences in moisture, temperature, and precipitation between the northeast and southwest were minimal.

title: WATERLINE
abstract: Hydrological models are an essential tool for water resources assessment and management. Advanced computational algorithms are capable of simulating the relevant physical processes and form the feedback mechanism across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. However, a bottleneck of these models is the lack of environmental observations to calibrate model parameters and to assess the robustness of model predictions. WATERLINE will employ multi-source information from remote sensing, historical data, in-situ data from meteorological networks as well as crowdsourced data to improve hydrological models and their predictions. The relevant physical processes and heterogeneity of hydrological catchments need to be integrated in hydrological models as a basis for reliable model predictions. A major challenge in this endeavour is identifying the observation data with the highest information content to constrain model parameters. Unfortunately, neither in-situ networks nor remote sensing alone can provide sufficient information to capture the high spatial and temporal variability of hydrological processes. Recently, downscaling frameworks have been developed, building robust models between coarse scale products and high-resolution ancillary variables using in-situ measurements. The lack of in-situ measurements to train such models can be overcome by the growing availability of crowdsourced observations. WATERLINE will improve the efficiency and robustness of hydrological models through strategic integration of variables covering different spatial and temporal scales. Furthermore, we will optimize the computational performances to provide near real-time and short-term predictions of various hydrological states with unprecedented spatial detail. Improved representation of soil moisture, groundwater levels and recharge, stream discharge, and evapotranspiration can significantly advance the sustainable management of water resources for a wide range of stakeholders. The WATERLINE concept will be implemented through development of a web services tool with three modular applications, targeting a) use by scientists (data access, downscaling, filtering, uncertainty analysis, modelling applications), b) use by non-technically trained stakeholders, providing enhanced visualization outputs, in the form of maps, graphs, indices enhanced with Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality functionalities, and c) crowdsourcing of hydrological information where a random user can report about any hydrological-related event and its severity using location-based service and textual input, which is then considered as an additional source of information for modelling and forecast estimation. User groups, such as farmers, water authorities, fire brigade services, entrepreneurs in tourist, agricultural, industrial sector will be actively involved in the development of the web-based interfaces to ensure the usability and adoption of the outcomes by relevant user communities.

title: Arctic_Soil_Properties _2149
abstract: This dataset contains lab-measured soil properties, including soil water matric potential, soil dielectric properties, soil electrical conductivity, and corresponding soil moisture levels. Additionally, it includes basic soil physical properties such as soil organic matter, bulk density, porosity, fiber content, root biomass, and mineral texture. Soil samples were collected from August 21 to August 27, 2018, from the surface down to the permafrost table in soil pits at nine sites along the Dalton Highway in northern and central Alaska. Permittivity and soil electrical conductivity measurements were conducted using METER TEROS 12 probes, while soil moisture measurements were made with a TEROS 21 probe. These measurements were performed in the lab over three years. The purpose of collecting and analyzing these soil samples was to develop an integrated framework relating the hydrological properties to the dielectric properties of the permafrost active layer soil, supporting the NASA Arctic and Boreal Vulnerability Experiment (ABoVE) Airborne Campaign.

title: North_Slope_Veg_Plots _1536
abstract: This dataset includes vegetation cover, environmental plot data, and soil data collected at flux tower sites of the North Slope Arctic System Science/Land-Atmosphere-Ice Interactions (ARCSS/LAII) project in August 1995 and 1996. The 19 flux tower sites are situated along a north-south transect from near Prudhoe Bay to the foothills of the Brooks Range on the North Slope of Alaska. Vegetation plots were established at 17 of the flux tower sites, totaling 29 plots. Measurements taken include (1) plant species cover for the major vegetation types using the Braun-Blanquet method, (2) plot environmental data, and (3) soil pro descriptions. Additionally, at all 19 sites, plant growth form composition and cover were assessed using a point sampling technique along multiple transects within selected plots.

abstract: Description The Arctic-Boreal Vulnerability Experiment (ABoVE) is a field campaign under NASA's Terrestrial Ecology Program. title: Flux_Tower_Zona_ Veg_Plots_1546
abstract: This dataset encompasses vegetation, environmental, and soil information gathered from plots within the footprints of eddy covariance flux towers, stretching over a 300 km north-south latitudinal gradient from Barrow to Atqasuk and Ivotuk on Alaska's North Slope in 2014. Within each of the five flux tower footprints, 1x1-meter quadrats were strategically placed in various habitat or micro-habitat types to map dominant vegetation communities and environmental factors. Key attributes recorded include species cover data along with environmental, soil, and spectral data such as active layer thaw depth, moss layer depth, organic horizon layer depth, standing water depth, soil moisture status, vegetation height, and leaf area index (LAI). Data collection occurred at three sites near Barrow: a well-drained wet coastal tundra site at the NOAA Climate Monitoring and Diagnostics Laboratory (US-Brw), a moderately well-drained wet coastal tundra site at the Barrow Environmental Observatory (US-Beo), and an inundated wet coastal tundra site at the southern end of the former Biocomplexity Experiment (US-Bes). The Atqasuk site (US-Atq) features sandy, non-acidic, moist tussock tundra, while the Ivotuk site (US-Ivo) is situated in the southern moist tussock tundra of the Brooks Range foothills.

title: Pingo_Veg_Plots_1507
abstract: This dataset comprises vegetation species and plot data collected in 1983 from 293 study plots on 41 pingos located on the North Slope of Alaska. The pingos are situated within the Arctic Coastal Plain, spanning the Kuparuk, Prudhoe Bay, Kadleroshilik, and Toolik River areas. Key attributes recorded include dominant vegetation species, vegetation cover, soil pH, soil moisture, and various physical characteristics of the plots. Pingos are ice-cored, dome-shaped mounds prevalent in permafrost regions and form a significant feature of the Alaskan central Arctic Coastal Plain landscape. A comprehensive list of plant species was cataloged for each plot. The vegetation patterns observed are complex, influenced by factors such as slope angle, slope aspect, wind effects, animal disturbances, site stability, snow deposition, and meso- and macroscale patterns related to the coastal climatic gradient and substrate variation.

title: FieldData_Alaska_ Tundra_2177
abstract: The Synthesized Alaskan Tundra Field Database (SATFiD) is a comprehensive compilation of in-situ field data drawn from 37 existing datasets, covering field surveys conducted at Alaskan tundra sites from 1972 to 2020. Prior to inclusion, the data were harmonized to ensure consistency. The dataset encompasses a variety of variables, including active layer thickness, vegetation cover (categorized by plant functional types), soil moisture, soil temperatures, and wildfire history. SATFiD offers valuable insights into long-term ecological processes in the tundra, such as the interactions between fire, permafrost, and vegetation, especially in the context of a rapidly changing climate.

title: Soil_Temp_Moisture _Alaska_1869
abstract: This dataset offers soil temperature and volumetric water content (VWC) measurements at a depth of 15 cm from 12 selected boreal and tundra sites spread across Alaska. At each site, there is a HOBO MicroStation Data Logger hosting two soil temperature sensors (HOBO S-TMB-M006 Temperature Smart Sensor) and two soil moisture sensors (HOBO S-SMD-M005 10HS Soil Moisture Smart Sensor). These sensors were installed horizontally within the soil pro. Samples of soil from seven sites underwent laboratory analysis to establish site-specific soil moisture sensor calibration curves, which were used to adjust raw measurements. The data were recorded nominally at an 1 hour frequency and downloaded from the sites at least annually from August 11, 2016, to September 2, 2023. However, data coverage varies by site.

title: Nome_Veg_Plots_1372
abstract: This dataset includes environmental, soil, and vegetation data collected from 80 study plots in the Nome River Valley, about 10 miles northeast of Nome, Alaska, on the Seward Peninsula, during July and August 1951. It provides baseline plot information on vegetation, soils, and site factors for these plots, which were subjectively located in plant communities across five broad habitat types within the glaciated landscape. title: Arctic_Network_Veg_ plots_1542
abstract: The Arctic-Boreal Vulnerability Experiment (ABoVE) is a field campaign under NASA's Terrestrial Ecology Program. The Arctic and Boreal regions are experiencing climate change more rapidly than any other place on the planet. ABoVE aims to gain a deeper understanding of how these ecosystems and human communities are vulnerable to, and can recover from, the impacts of this swiftly changing environment. This dataset comprises environmental, soil, and vegetation data collected at specific locations within the National Park Service (NPS) Arctic Network (ARCN) parks and preserves between 2002 and 2008. The ARCN encompasses five national parks and preserves in northern Alaska, covering 19.5 million acres of some of the most pristine and undisturbed areas on Earth. These parks and preserves include the Bering Land Bridge National Preserve, Cape Krusenstern National Monument, Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve, Kobuk Valley National Park, and the Noatak National Preserve.

title: PTSMN
abstract: 20 probes (4 sensors/unit) were installed in predominantly silt loam soils on a pastoral hill country farm on the southern east coast of the North Island of New Zealand. Over a one-year period (01/11/2016 ? 01/12/2017), raw sensor readings and those derived from a manufacturer-recommended calibration were compared with 400 reference measurements. Additionally, three custom calibration methods were developed and assessed, tailored to the available soil information. The sensors' temporal responses closely agreed with the magnitude of rainfall events. However, performance and accuracy varied with soil wetness, bulk density, clay content, and total organic carbon (TOC). Increased clay content and bulk density resulted in higher raw output for a given moisture level, whereas TOC showed the opposite trend. These effects were significant (P value?<?0.001) but were mitigated by sensor-specific custom calibration.

title: AWDN
abstract: The AWDN is a cooperative effort, which is made possible by partnerships with six state-run mesonet programs across the High Plains region. The primary function of the AWDN is to aggregate and quality control the data from these discrete networks in order to create regional products that can then be used for various sectors, such as agriculture and water resources. Current and/or archived observations from over 350 stations are available across the nine states of Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, and Wyoming. The North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network (NDAWN) is managed by the NDAWN Center at North Dakota State University. The network was established in the late 1980s with a grant from the HPRCC. Since that time, NDAWN has grown to be one of the largest networks in the region, with over 90 stations across North Dakota, Minnesota, and Montana. NDAWN provides a wide range of tools, including: Deep Soil Temperature Measurements Numerous Agricultural Tools (Crop and Insect GDD, Crop Water Use, etc.) Soil Moisture, Temperature Inversion Dat, and Wind Chill.

title: TxSON
abstract: The Texas Soil Observation Network (TxSON) is a state-of-the-art network of stations designed to monitor soil water content, surface and ground water, and meteorological variables across various locations in Texas. Initially deployed in 2015, it began with 40 stations within a ~36 km² grid near Fredericksburg, TX, along the Pedernales River and the middle reaches of the Colorado River. Since then, the network has expanded to include additional stations monitoring weather and soil conditions in other areas of Texas, such as the greater Houston area, Marfa, and Brady. TxSON also operates three stations that monitor water quality and spring flow at natural springs in West Texas, near Fort Stockton and Balmorhea. Furthermore, it maintains two stations near San Antonio that measure water vapor and carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes using the eddy covariance (EC) technique. TxSON serves as a Core Calibration and Validation Site for NASA's Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission, as well as for the European Space Agency's (ESA) Soil Moisture Ocean Salinity (SMOS) mission and Sentinel-1 satellites.

title: AirMOSS_Field_Data_ Harvard_1677
abstract: This dataset provides in situ measurements of soil temperature, moisture, conductivity, and tree measurements, including diameter at breast height (DBH) and total height, collected at the Harvard Forest in Petersham, Massachusetts, USA. The data were gathered in October 2012 and from July to August 2013. These measurements support the Airborne Microwave Observatory of Subcanopy and Subsurface (AirMOSS) project, which aims to validate root-zone soil moisture measurements and carbon flux model estimates. Soil measurements were taken from established plots along two transects during 2012 and 2013 at depth ranging from 5.8 cm to 20 cm. Soil temperature was specifically measured at approximately 5.8 cm depth. DBH measurements for various tree species were conducted in October 2012. Additionally, hemispherical canopy photographs were taken for each plot to complement the dataset.

title: ALT_GPR_Barrow_1355
abstract: The Arctic-Boreal Vulnerability Experiment (ABoVE) is a field campaign under NASA's Terrestrial Ecology Program. The Arctic and Boreal regions are experiencing climate change more rapidly than any other place on the planet. ABoVE aims to gain a deeper understanding of how these ecosystems and human communities are vulnerable to, and can recover from, the impacts of this swiftly changing environment. This dataset offers estimates of Active Layer Thickness (ALT) derived from ground-based measurements and calculated soil volumetric water content (VWC) at four sites around Barrow, Alaska, in August 2013. VWC of the active layer soil was calculated at 3 to 8 calibration points per site, where probe measurements were precisely co-located with GPR traces. Data collection took place in August, coinciding with the period when the active layer generally reaches its maximum thickness.

title: Nongrowing_Season_ CO2_Flux_1692
abstract: This dataset provides a comprehensive synthesis of winter (September-April) in situ soil CO2 flux measurements from various locations across the pan-Arctic and Boreal permafrost regions. Compiled from 66 published and 21 unpublished studies conducted between 1989 and 2017, the dataset includes detailed publication references for data sources. Sampling sites encompass pan-Arctic Boreal and tundra regions (north of 53° N) across continuous, discontinuous, and isolated/sporadic permafrost zones. The CO2 flux measurements are aggregated at the 1 month level, or seasonally when 1 month data were unavailable, and reported as 1 day averages (g C m?² day?¹) over the specified intervals. The dataset also includes soil moisture and temperature data, along with environmental and ecological model driver data such as vegetation type, productivity, and soil substrate availability. These additional data are derived from gridded satellite remote sensing and reanalysis sources.

title: LUYSSAERT_CARBON _FLUX_949
abstract: A comprehensive global database has been assembled to quantify CO2 fluxes and pathways at various levels of integration?from photosynthesis to net ecosystem production?in forest ecosystems. This database is essential for model calibration, validation, and hypothesis testing at global and regional scales. The database archive includes (1) a Microsoft Office Access Database, (2) data s for all tables in the database, (3) query outputs from the database, and (4) an SQL script for recreating the database from the tables. The database is organized by site, each representing a forest or stand with known geographical location, biome, species composition, and management regime. The database comprises information from 529 sites across eight forest biomes. Data entries originate from peer-reviewed literature and personal communications with researchers involved in Fluxnet. Flux estimates included are based on direct measurements (e.g., tower-based eddy covariance system measurements), derived from single or multiple direct measurements, or modeled. Stand descriptions are based on observed values, while climatic descriptions are based on the CRU data set and ORCHIDEE model output.

title: Arctic_Boreal_CO2_ Flux_1934
abstract: The Arctic-Boreal CO2 fluxes (ABCflux) dataset features 1 month aggregates of terrestrial net ecosystem CO2 exchange, along with its partitioned component fluxes: gross primary productivity (GPP) and ecosystem respiration. This dataset is enriched with over 70 supporting variables that detail key site conditions (such as vegetation and disturbance type), micrometeorological data, and environmental measurements (including air and soil temperatures), as well as the techniques used for flux measurement. The ABCflux dataset is a standardized 1 month database encompassing CO2 fluxes across Arctic-Boreal regions. It includes data from 244 sites and 6,309 1 month observations, with 136 sites and 2,217 observations representing tundra, and 108 sites and 4,092 observations representing the boreal biome. The data spans the period from 1989 to 2020.

title: S2k_mongu_soil_prop_789
abstract: Soil moisture and temperature pro sensors were installed at flux tower sites in Mongu, Zambia, and Skukuza, South Africa. Additionally, thermal infrared sensors were used to monitor surface temperature at these sites, and soil samples were collected for physical property analysis. A heat-flux plate was placed at a depth of 10 cm at the Mongu site. Data were collected from August 1999 to December 2001. At the Mongu site, three soil moisture and temperature pros were measured to a maximum depth of 125 cm, located approximately 30 meters north of the Mongu flux tower within the Kataba Local Forest. Surface radiometric temperature was recorded by thermal infrared sensors positioned on top of the 30-meter tower and on a tree. At the Skukuza site, two pros of soil moisture and temperature were measured to a maximum depth of 40 cm in a Combretum stand. Infrared thermocouple sensors on a pole at 2.5 m and 5 m heights monitored the radiometric temperature of the tree crown and the background surface.

title: RUSWET-VALDAI
abstract: Soil moisture datasets for 3 catchments located at the Valdai basin were collected by the State Hydrological Institute in St. Petersburg from 1960 to 1990. The catchments differ in their vegetation, Usadievskiy has mostly grassland vegetation, Tayozhniy a mature forest and Sinaya Gnilka was articifally forested in 1961. The soil moisture was computed by using data from 9-11 observational points distributed over the basin area. The resulting files contain monthly means of soil moisture for the layers of 0-20, 0-50 and 0-100 cm. These files were downloaded from the \Global Soil Moisture Database\" and transformed into volumetric soil moisture [m^3/m^3]. Thus soil moisture values are available as monthly means

title: RUSWET-GRASS
abstract: This network combines the two datasets RUSWET-GRASS-50STA and RUSWET-GRASS-130STA of the Global Soil Moisture Data Bank by Alan Robock and Konstantin Vinnikov. Soil moisture information at 122 meterological stations of the Former Soviet Union were collected. The results of soil moisture gravimetric measurements, which were taken at plots with natural grass type vegetation, were initially provided as volumetric plant-available water [%]. Volumetric soil moisture [m^3/m^3] was calculated by first extracting texture properties of all sites from the Harmonized World Soil Database and subsequently calculating the wilting levels for all stations using the equations of Saxton and Rawls (2006). For the period 1952 to 1985 soil moisture measurements for the layer 0-100 cm are provided for some stations. Measurements of the upper 10 cm soil layer are available for the period 1977 to 1985.

abstract: Soil moisture datasets for 78 districts have been prepared by Vladimir Zabelin from the Russian Hydrometeorological Center, Moscow, Russia. The soil moisture observations were taken using the gravimetric technique and were provided as volumetric plant-available water [%] for the upper 20 cm and 1 m soil layers at agricultural fields. Thus volumetric soil moisture [m^3/m^3] was calculated by first extracting texture properties of all sites from the Harmonized World Soil Database and subsequently calculating the wilting levels for all stations using the equations of Saxton and Rawls (2006). As this dataset was designed for monitoring of soil moisture at agricultural fields datasets were seperately available for spring cereal crops and winter cereal crops for all locations. In the ISMN stations with the suffix \a\" represent spring cereal crops while stations with \"b\" illustrate winter cereal crops. Measurements are available during the growing period from 1987 to 1988

title: Pre_LBA_ABRACOS_899
abstract: The dataset presents primary data from the Anglo-Brazilian Amazonian Climate Observation Study (ABRACOS), offering quality-controlled information across five study topics within five zipped s containing ASCII text data. These topics encompass Micrometeorology, Climate, Carbon Dioxide and Water Vapor, Plant Physiology, and Soil Moisture. ABRACOS aimed to monitor the Amazonian climate, enhance comprehension of deforestation consequences, and provide data for calibrating and validating General Circulation Models (GCMs) and GCM sub-models of Amazonian forest and post-deforestation pasture. Instrumentation was deployed in three areas, each characterized by distinct soils, dry season intensities, and deforestation densities. Within each area, automatic weather stations and soil moisture measurement equipment were installed in primary forest sites and adjacent cattle pastures to monitor climate and soil conditions throughout the year. Additionally, intensive study periods (Missions) of varying duration were conducted at these sites for calibration purposes, understanding site-specific physical processes, and detailed inter-site comparisons. These data were collected under the ABRACOS project and are made available by the UK Institute of Hydrology and the Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Brazil). ABRACOS is a collaboration between the Agencia Brasileira de Cooperacao and the UK Overseas Development Administration. The processed, quality-controlled, and integrated data in the documented Pre-LBA datasets were initially published as three CD-ROMs (Marengo and Victoria, 1998) but are now archived individually.

title: Wildfires_NWT_Canada _2019_1900
abstract: This dataset furnishes data on vegetation community characteristics, soil moisture, and biophysical attributes collected in 2019 across 11 study areas encompassing 28 sites affected by wildfires in 2014 and 2015, as well as 14 unburned sites in the Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada. The burned sites include both peatland and upland areas. Field data encompass vegetation inventories, ground cover assessments, as well as tree and shrub diameter and height measurements for unburned sites. Similar data were gathered for the unburned sites in the years 2015-18 and are accessible in related separate datasets. In 2019, particular emphasis was placed on collecting data related to woody and non-woody seedling/sprouting regrowth in the burned sites. Additional measurements conducted at all sites include total peat depth, soil moisture, and active layer thickness (ALT). Soil moisture and ALT measurements were collected to validate UAVSAR airborne collection and Radarsat-2 overpasses. The fieldwork conducted in 2019 marks the culmination of five years of field sampling at the wildfire-affected areas.

title: SNEX_Met
abstract: This dataset comprises meteorological data gathered as part of the ongoing NASA SnowEx mission. Five meteorological stations were installed between 2016 and 2017 in Grand Mesa, Colorado, to supply supporting data for SnowEx field campaigns and serve as forcing data for modeling efforts. Each station is positioned at a fixed geographic point and records a range of meteorological variables from various heights above and below the surface elevation. The measured data include air temperature, relative humidity, longwave and shortwave solar radiation, barometric pressure, soil moisture and temperature, as well as derived snow depth. Temporal coverage varies among the stations but generally spans from October 2016 to August 2022. The dataset provides information such as air temperature and relative humidity at 10ft and 20ft levels, four-component radiation (shortwave and longwave), barometric pressure, soil moisture and temperature at three depth, and a snow depth product. Data frequency is 1 hour, and timestamps are provided in UTC. The dataset is quality-controlled, ensuring monotonicity without duplicate or misordered timestamps. Any periods of missing data are filled with NaN values.

title: SV19MA_VOD
abstract: During the SMAPVEX19-21 campaign, an L-band radiometer was positioned atop a tower at Harvard Forest in Massachusetts, observing a stand of red oak forest. The radiometer operated in V-polarization mode from late April to mid-October 2019. Additionally, measurements of water potential and the L-band complex dielectric constant of canopy leaves were conducted over four days in early July 2019 at various times throughout the day. Several other instruments were deployed within the radiometer's field of view to gather complementary data, including soil moisture and temperature sensors, air temperature monitors, tree xylem apparent dielectric permittivity at 70 MHz sensors, tree xylem water potential gauges, and canopy wetness sensors. The primary objective of this experiment was to investigate the sensitivity of L-band vegetation optical depth (VOD) to variations in vegetation water potential over the course of a growing season.

title: FIFE_PECK_SM_109
abstract: Water content measurements by Gravimetric methodss involve weighing a wet soil sample, drying it in an oven to remove the water, and then reweighing the dry sample. The amount of water removed is determined by the difference between the wet and dry masses. The water content is calculated by dividing this difference by the mass of the dry sample, yielding the ratio of the mass of water to the mass of dry soil. Multiplying this ratio by 100 provides the percentage of water in the sample on a dry-mass (or dry-weight) basis. Using the Gravimetric methods, soil moisture was measured at 800 sites along 24 transects, which were also overflown by the airborne Gamma Radiation System to measure soil moisture. These ground measurements are crucial for comparing with airborne data. Analysis using these independent soil moisture data showed that the airborne Gamma Radiation System had a root mean square error of 3.02 percent soil moisture across 97 flights, with a bias of less than 0.5 percent soil moisture (Carroll et al., 1988).

title: FIFE_SM_GRAV_110
abstract: Gravimetric soil moisture data were collected from numerous stations across the FIFE study area. These data aimed to characterize the spatial and temporal patterns of soil moisture during and between the FIFE Intensive Field Campaigns. The objectives of the FIFE soil moisture work included: 1. Characterizing the spatial and temporal patterns of soil moisture at the FIFE site. 2. Validating and calibrating remote sensing measurements of soil moisture. 3. Evaluating alternative methods of measuring soil moisture both from the air and on the ground. 4. Developing techniques to compare point measurements with spatially continuous measurements of soil moisture. The FIFE soil moisture research was designed to advance technology for soil moisture characterization and provide valuable data for other FIFE investigations.

title: FIFE_SOIL_GAS_106
abstract: This dataset contains 1 day flux rates of denitrification, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide obtained from 10 sites during four sampling dates in 1987. Samples were taken in and around six of the FIFE study sites. It includes estimates of in situ fluxes and denitrification fluxes measured in cores amended with either water or water plus nitrate. Detailed analyses of the relationships between 1 day flux rates and soil moisture, and between annual fluxes and plant productivity, are reported in other works (Groffman and Turner, submitted to Ecology; Groffman and Wood, in preparation). Additionally, the denitrification data and the evaluation of denitrification fluxes within the ecosystem ecology context of the FIFE study area are presented in Groffman et al. (1992).

title: FIFE_SM_NEUT_111
abstract: The neutron-probe data consist of a series of measurements of volumetric water content in the soil pro, compiled using the neutron method. These data were collected across the FIFE study area from May 1987 through August 1989. The neutron method for measuring soil water content is based on the principle of neutron thermalization. Water, which contains hydrogen and oxygen, significantly slows down or thermalizes neutrons. Thermal neutron density, easily measured with a detector, can be calibrated against water concentration on a volume basis, provided the capture cross-section remains constant.

title: FIFE_SM_TRAN_113
abstract: The objective of the FIFE soil moisture transect work was to characterize the spatial and temporal patterns of soil moisture along selected transects within the FIFE study area. This effort supported the passive microwave (PBMR) flights over the Konza experimental area by collecting two levels of ground data. Water content measurements were gathered using Gravimetric methodss. Measuring soil moisture along a transect is essential for calibrating airborne moisture instruments or comparing the data obtained from them. Due to the inherent heterogeneity of soil units in a landscape, moisture content can vary along the aircraft flight path on the ground. To minimize errors, samples were taken at close intervals along the flight path.

title: FIFE_SOILTHER_116
abstract: The 1989 FIFE soil properties investigation aimed to describe the thermal properties of soils within the FIFE study area. Soil thermal conductivity measurements were taken to understand the soil properties that influence heat flow through the soil. Thermal conductivity is defined as the amount of heat that flows through a unit area in a unit time under a unit temperature gradient. These measurements were conducted in situ at two depth across 26 FIFE sites in October 1987, using a hot wire probe method. This method involves placing a long, electrically heated wire inside a cylindrical probe inserted into the soil. The wire is heated by an electric current, and the temperature rise is measured with a thermocouple adjacent to the wire. The thermal conductivity is derived from a plot of temperature versus the logarithm of time. The results may need a correction factor to account for the probe's dimensions.

title: AirMOSS_L2_Inground_ Soil_Moist_1416
abstract: This data set provides level 2 (L2) 1 hour volumetric (cm3/cm3) soil moisture pros from in-ground sensors at seven North American sites as part of the Airborne Microwave Observatory of Subcanopy and Subsurface (AirMOSS) project. Three pros were installed at each site, sampling at seven different depth per pro (2 cm to 80 cm). Initial sampling began at three sites in September 2011 and additional sites were added during 2012 and 2013. All sampling concluded in December 2015. The AirMOSS project used an airborne radar instrument to estimate root-zone soil moisture at 10 study sites across North America. These in-ground soil moisture data were collected to calibrate and validate the AirMOSS data. goal of NASA?s Airborne Microwave Observatory of Subcanopy and Subsurface (AirMOSS) investigation is to provide high-resolution observations of root-zone soil moisture over regions representative of the major North American climatic habitats (biomes), quantify the impact of variations in soil moisture on the estimation of regional carbon fluxes, and extrapolate the reduced-uncertainty estimates of regional carbon fluxes to the continental scale of North America. The AirMOSS campaign used an airborne ultra-high frequency synthetic aperture radar flown on a Gulfstream-III aircraft to derive estimates of soil moisture down to approximately 1.2 meters. Extensive ground, tower, and aircraft in-situ measurements were collected to validate root-zone soil measurements and carbon flux model estimates. The AirMOSS soil measurements can be used to better understand carbon fluxes and their associated uncertainties on a continental scale. Additionally, AirMOSS data provide a direct means for validating root-zone soil measurement algorithms from the Soil Moisture Active & Passive (SMAP)

title: SoilSCAPE_1339
abstract: This dataset encompasses in-situ soil moisture pro and soil temperature data collected at 20-minute intervals across various SoilSCAPE (Soil moisture Sensing Controller and oPtimal Estimator) project sites situated in four states within the United States: California, Arizona, Oklahoma, and Michigan. Leveraging wireless sensor technology, SoilSCAPE enables the acquisition of high temporal resolution soil moisture and temperature data from up to 12 sites, with data collection spanning since August 2011. At its peak, the network comprised over 200 wireless sensor installations (nodes), with each site hosting between 6 to 27 nodes. Soil moisture sensors, including EC-5 and 5-TM from Decagon Devices, were strategically placed at depth ranging from 5 to 50 centimeters below the surface, with sensor placement potentially constrained by soil conditions such as hard soil or rocks. Additionally, temperature sensors were deployed at a depth of 5 centimeters at six of the sites. Data collection commenced in August 2011 and persists at eight sites to date. This dataset facilitates the estimation of local-scale soil moisture at high temporal resolution and serves as a means for validating remote sensing estimates of soil moisture at regional (e.g., airborne missions like NASA's Airborne Microwave Observation of Subcanopy and Subsurface Mission - AirMOSS) and national (e.g., spaceborne missions like NASA's Soil Moisture Active Passive - SMAP) scales.

title: AACES
abstract: The AACES campaigns were designed to cover a large part of the Murrumbidgee River catchment capturing summer (AACES-1) and winter conditions (AACES-2). Given the approximately 50 km sized SMOS pixels, the study transect had been aligned with the SMOS fixed grid and subdivided into ten patches of approximately 100 km × 50 km in size, of which each had been mapped within a single day. The airborne observations were undertaken at approximately 3000 m (AGL) altitude to provide passive microwave data and derived soil moisture content with a 1 km spatial resolution. The primary aircraft instrument was the PLMR, used in across-track configuration (pushbroom) to map the surface with three viewing angles ( ±7°, ±21.5° and ±38.5°) to each side of the flight direction, achieving a swath width of about 6 km. The two field experiments, ACCES-1 (18 January to 21 February, 2010) and AACES-2 (8 to 26 September, 2010) have been successfully conducted and the collected data sets, sampling strategies and ancillary information are described in detail on the individual websites which can be accessed via the links below.
